title: Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v. ROSS Intelligence Inc. — Memorandum Opinion on Renewed Summary Judgment (D. Del., Bibas, J.)
pub: U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware, No. 1:20-cv-613-SB, Dkt. 770; 765 F. Supp. 3d 382
author: Stephanos Bibas

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses copyright infringement and fair use in training a competing non-generative legal-research system, not task-level capability, human verification, selective deployment or operating-model redesign. Its explicit limitation to non-generative AI further prevents treating it as evidence for or against the cluster’s proposition.
qs: Because the AI landscape is changing rapidly, I  note for readers that only non-generative AI is before me today.
Ross was using Thomson Reuters’s headnotes as AI data to create a legal research  tool to compete with Westlaw.

st.t: AI copyright: Product purpose reshapes market harm
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s case-specific framework. It rejects fair use because ROSS’s non-generative legal-search product shared Westlaw’s purpose and was intended as a market substitute, while expressly limiting its reasoning to the particular non-generative system before the court rather than declaring AI training categorically unlawful.
qs: Ross’s use is not transformative because it does  not have a “further purpose or different character” from Thomson Reuters’s.
Because the AI landscape is changing rapidly, I  note for readers that only non-generative AI is before me today.

st.t: Training fair use: Lawfulness depends on particular copying
st.an: The ruling directly supports the synthesis’s use-specific approach: it denies fair use because ROSS used protected headnotes for the commercial purpose of developing a competing legal-research product, while expressly limiting its reasoning to non-generative AI. It also supplies one side of the cluster’s market-harm dispute by treating competition with Westlaw and a potential legal-AI training-data market as cognizable harm despite nonpublic outputs.
qs: Ross took the headnotes to make it easier to develop a competing legal research tool.
And it does not matter whether Thomson Reuters has used the data to train its  own legal search tools; the effect on a potential market for AI training data is enough.

mo.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control

ROSS shutdown: Litigation can eliminate unresolved competitors

kp.k: Competing legal AI relied on incumbent editorial training data
kp.d: The opinion describes Ross developing an AI legal-research search engine that competed with Westlaw. After Thomson Reuters refused a licence because Ross was a competitor, Ross obtained roughly 25,000 Bulk Memos from LegalEase to train its tool. These lawyer-produced legal questions and answers were built using Westlaw headnotes; LegalEase instructed lawyers not simply to copy and paste the headnotes. This is the court's account of the disputed product-development process, not a general finding about legal AI development.
qs: So Ross asked to license Westlaw’s content.
But  because Ross was its competitor, Thomson Reuters refused.
In other words, Ross built  its competing product using Bulk Memos, which in turn were built from Westlaw  headnotes.

kp.k: Ruling expressly concerns retrieval AI, not generative AI
kp.d: The court distinguishes Ross's retrieval system, which returned existing judicial opinions in response to legal questions, from generative AI that writes new content. Its comparison with Westlaw rests on both tools helping researchers find relevant cases. The judge expressly limits the decision's technological scope to non-generative AI.
qs: It is undisputed that Ross’s AI is not generative AI (AI  that writes new content itself).
Rather, when a user enters a legal question, Ross spits  back relevant judicial opinions that have already been written.
only non-generative AI is before me today.

kp.k: Editorial selection qualifies for copyright protection
kp.d: Revising his 2023 analysis, Judge Bibas finds that Westlaw headnotes and the Key Number System satisfy copyright's minimal originality threshold. Although judicial opinions themselves are not copyrightable, selecting, distilling and arranging their legal propositions can express editorial judgment. He treats individual headnotes, including verbatim selections, as original works, while distinguishing originality from proof that Ross copied them; he does not grant infringement summary judgment for headnotes that merely reproduce opinion text verbatim.
qs: The text of judicial opinions is not copyrightable.
But a headnote  can introduce creativity by distilling, synthesizing, or explaining part of an opinion,  and thus be copyrightable.
So all headnotes, even any that  quote judicial opinions verbatim, have original value as individual works.
There are many possible, logical ways to organize legal topics by level  of granularity. It is enough that Thomson Reuters chose a particular one.

kp.k: Court finds infringement of 2,243 headnotes, with qualifications
kp.d: Following comparisons of Bulk Memo questions, headnotes and underlying judicial opinions, the court grants partial summary judgment on actual copying and substantial similarity for 2,243 headnotes. It confines this determination to instances where no reasonable jury could disagree. Copyright coverage and validity questions remain for trial, including expiration or untimely creation; other headnotes and disputed uses of the Key Number System and editorial decisions in 500 opinions are not finally resolved by this ruling.
qs: Ross infringed 2,243 headnotes.
The rest  of the headnotes must go to trial.
I do not decide at summary judgment the factual ques-  tion of which headnotes are still covered by Thomson Reuters’s existing copyrights  and leave this question open for trial.
There are still factual dis-  putes about whether Ross used it and how

kp.k: Intermediate training use was not transformative here
kp.d: The court finds Ross's use commercial and non-transformative because it used headnotes to develop a competing legal-research tool serving a similar purpose. It acknowledges that headnotes were converted into numerical relationship data and did not appear in the consumer product. Nevertheless, it distinguishes software intermediate-copying precedents: the copied material here was not computer code, and copying was not necessary to reach otherwise inaccessible underlying ideas. This is a case-specific fair-use determination, not a holding about all AI training.
qs: Ross’s use is commercial.
Ross’s use is not transformative.
the headnotes do not appear as part of the final product that  Ross put forward to consumers.
Ross took the headnotes to make it easier to develop a competing legal research tool.
Here, though, there is no computer code whose underlying ideas can be reached only  by copying their expression.

kp.k: Limited creativity and undisclosed headnotes favored Ross
kp.d: Fair-use factors two and three favor Ross. The court finds that headnotes involve editorial creativity but less than works created from scratch, and that the Key Number System has limited creativity as a factual compilation. For factor three, it emphasizes that Ross did not expose headnotes to the public, rather than the volume copied during training. It rejects Ross's separate argument that copying only a small percentage of Westlaw's total headnotes necessarily supports fair use.
qs: But the material is not that creative.
And the Key Number System is a factual compilation,  so its creativity is limited.
Because Ross did not  make West headnotes available to the public, Ross benefits from factor three.
The percentage of a total work copied is neither  necessary nor sufficient to decide factor three.

kp.k: Potential AI training markets weigh against fair use
kp.d: The court identifies both legal-research platforms and a potential derivative market for legal-AI training data as relevant to market harm. It finds that Ross intended to develop a Westlaw substitute and holds that potential training-data market effects matter even without proof that Thomson Reuters already trained its own tools on the data. Ross, bearing the affirmative-defense burden, had not supplied enough facts to negate those market effects. This is a legal assessment of potential markets, not a measurement of actual lost revenue.
qs: The original  market is obvious: legal-research platforms.
And at least one potential derivative  market is also obvious: data to train legal AIs.
the effect on a potential market for AI training data is enough.
Ross bears the burden of proof. It has not put forward enough facts to show that these markets do not exist and would not be affected.

kp.k: Public legal access does not confer editorial-content rights
kp.d: The judge recognizes the public interest in accessing law but distinguishes freely available judicial opinions from Thomson Reuters's proprietary editorial treatment. He argues that copyright rewards the creation of useful research tools and that Ross could have developed its own material without infringement. Public benefit therefore does not overcome the market and purpose considerations in this case. On balance, factors one and four outweigh factors two and three, defeating Ross's fair-use defense.
qs: Yes, there is a public interest  in accessing the law.
The public  has no right to Thomson Reuters’s parsing of the law.
Copyrights encourage people  to develop things that help society, like good legal-research tools.
Factors one and four favor Thomson Reuters. Factors two and three favor Ross.
Weighing them  all together, I grant summary judgment for Thomson Reuters on fair use.

kp.d: The court rejects innocent infringement, copyright misuse, merger and scenes à faire. It explains that innocent infringement concerns damages rather than liability and is unavailable here because the headnotes carry copyright notices. Ross had not shown anticompetitive copyright misuse; legal propositions admit multiple expressions, defeating merger; and the nature of judicial opinions does not require Westlaw's particular editorial condensation or categorization.
qs: Ross’s innocent infringement, copyright misuse, merger, and scenes à faire            defenses all fail.
innocent infringement does not limit liability, just  damages.
Ross has not shown that Thomson Reuters misused its copyrights to stifle  competition.
there are many ways  to express points of law from judicial opinions

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Bibas characterizes ROSS’s non-generative AI research tool as a competitive substitute for Westlaw and identifies legal-AI training data as a potential derivative market.
pts.d: In this February 2025 opinion, Bibas describes AI-enabled competition in legal research rather than forecasting lawyer displacement or productivity gains. ROSS used training materials derived from Westlaw headnotes to develop a tool returning relevant judicial opinions. Bibas concludes that this commercial, competing use was not transformative and rejects ROSS’s fair-use defense, even though users did not receive the headnotes themselves. He also concludes that potential effects on a market for AI training data matter regardless of whether Thomson Reuters had already used its data to train its own tools.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on the litigation record, judicial comparison of training materials with headnotes and opinions, and copyright doctrine—not AI-performance benchmarks or measured market losses.
pts.d: Bibas relies on the parties’ agreement that the products compete, the record describing LegalEase’s production of roughly 25,000 Bulk Memos, ROSS counsel’s account of training and validation use, and an expert report concerning textual resemblance. He also compares the materials himself and finds actual copying and substantial similarity for 2,243 headnotes. His market analysis is a legal assessment of substitution and potential derivative markets, supported by fair-use authorities and ROSS’s failure to carry its burden; the opinion does not quantify revenue losses, research efficiency, or AI accuracy.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The opinion resolves aspects of an existing dispute as of February 11, 2025; it expressly limits its AI analysis to non-generative AI.
pts.d: Bibas revises his 2023 summary-judgment analysis rather than offering a dated forecast of industry change. The ruling concerns commercial use of protected editorial material to develop a competing research tool, not all AI training. He distinguishes intermediate copying precedents involving computer code and copying necessary to reach underlying ideas. Copyright-validity questions for individual headnotes remain for trial, as do other infringement questions. The training-data market is expressly potential rather than established through quantified transactions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are legal-research platform owners, competing AI vendors, training-data suppliers, legal researchers, and the public seeking access to law.
pts.d: Thomson Reuters is treated as both an incumbent research-platform owner and a rights holder with a potential AI-training-data market. ROSS is a competing legal-tech vendor, not an alternative legal service provider; its use of headnote-derived training materials exposes it to copyright liability and an unsuccessful fair-use defense. LegalEase supplied the intermediate training materials. Researchers are the users of competing case-retrieval tools. Bibas acknowledges the public interest in accessing law but distinguishes freely available opinions from proprietary editorial treatment, presenting copyright protection as an incentive to build research tools rather than finding a measured access-to-justice benefit.
